article.articleHeadline: Kerala sees HIV surge among men in their 20s | Part 1
article.articleSummary:
- Kerala reports rising HIV infections among youths, driven by men who have sex with men (MSM). In 2025-2026, MSM accounted for 29% of new HIV-positive individuals enrolled at Care and Support Centres (CSCs); in the first quarter of the current financial year, 31% were MSM. The 15–24 age group rose from 9% of new infections in 2022 to 14.2% in 2024, and 15.4% between April–October 2025. District data show: Kasaragod—52 new cases in 2025-2026, with seven of the first three months’ 10 cases MSM (two were students); Palakkad—120 new cases, 38 MSM; Kollam and Thiruvananthapuram—426 new cases, 155 MSM, of whom 115 were 24 or younger; Ernakulam and Thrissur—417 new cases at Thrissur CSC, 116 MSM, 29 injection drug users. Counsellors note underreporting due to anonymity; many MSM meet partners onli
- HIV misinformation in Karnataka was rejected by NACO; Health Minister U. T. Khader stated in Bengaluru that NACO’s figure of 56,000 cases is not accepted, clarifying that a false report suggested about 7,000 college students were HIV positive. The health department is prepared to issue a clarification. Since 2004, Karnataka has recorded 39,028 HIV infections; 18–35-year-olds are receiving treatment. HIV testing is conducted in only two settings: during pregnancy and when blood is donated. Officials say the state’s HIV situation is under control. In the last three months, 3,091 infections were detected among 553,453 people tested, and 281,742 pregnant women were tested for HIV in the same period, indicating ongoing surveillance and targeted testing in Karnataka.

- Rubella cases rise in Bantul Regency, Indonesia, prompting strengthened prevention via School Immunization Month (BIAS) beginning August 2026. Measles-Rubella (MR) vaccine will be administered to nine‑month-olds, 18-month-olds, and primary school students according to the national schedule, with phased distribution to puskesmas; phase one already in August and phase two in November. article.articleHeadline: World Hepatitis Day celebration: In Jamnagar, 150 UG-PG scholars were given detailed information about Hepatitis B and C in the IT room.
article.articleSummary: World Hepatitis Day was celebrated in Jamnagar by the municipal health department under the theme 'Let's Break It Down' at ITRA, informing approximately 150 undergraduate and postgraduate scholars about Hepatitis B and C in the IT room. Dr. Hareshkumar Gori and city health officer Dr. Palak Ganatra guided the program with support from ITRA's director. Prof. Ami Trivedi, General Medicine and MTC-NVHVP nodal officer, delivered detailed information on Hepatitis B and C—types, symptoms, prevention, vaccination importance, and government-funded free treatment and services. Dean Dr. Nandini Desai attended. IEC materials were displayed to promote awareness in simple language, with Lions Club members also participating. The session noted Hepatitis A and E spread mainly through contaminated water or food, typically causing short-term illness that resolves with proper care. The aim was public awareness, timely diagnosis and treatment, and encouragement of healthy lifestyles.

article.articleHeadline: India approves QDENGA dengue vaccine; rollout still months away
article.articleSummary: India approves manufacture of QDENGA dengue vaccine, the world's first widely approved dengue vaccine, offering prevention to crores of people in India where dengue resurges each monsoon. The Drug Controller General of India has cleared production of QDENGA, signaling a shift after decades dominated by mosquito control, public awareness campaigns, and supportive treatment. The vaccine’s introduction promises prevention rather than cure and could become a key tool against one of India's fastest-growing seasonal health threats. Rollout remains months away, with supply and distribution likely to shape the timetable. This development highlights the seasonality of dengue in India and the potential to reduce the annual disease burden once manufacturing and deployment scale up across affected regions.

article.articleSummary: Malaria outbreak triggers a high-alert response in the Achanakmar Tiger Reserve area under Lormi block, Mungeli district, India. District Collector Kundan Kumar has ordered a wide-ranging malaria-control campaign emphasizing timely diagnosis and treatment to curb transmission. Administrative and health teams are conducting door-to-door surveys and visits to Tilaidabara, Bahoud, Sarasdol, Jamunahi, Atariyakhār, and Rajk villages to assess conditions, provide care, and ensure uninterrupted services. The health department reports all malaria patients are receiving treatment; severe cases are admitted to health facilities, while others are under regular monitoring. Rapid diagnostic test kits and anti-malarial medicines are stocked with frontline workers, including mitanins, for on-the-spot testing and treatment. A control room for continuous surveillance of malaria and other seasonal illnesses has been established. Authorities urge residents to wear long-sleeved clothing, use mosquito nets, keep surroundings clean, and drink boiled or safe water.

article.articleHeadline: Bitten by a wolf; life lost despite rabies vaccination; CPR performed: the unfortunate farmer from Arjunwada
article.articleSummary: Dileep Dasharat Yadav, 56, a farmer from Arjunwada in Raadhanagari Taluka, Kolhapur district, died during treatment after a wolf bite on November 12, 2025. He sustained a fractured thumb in the attack while drying pajar in his field. He was admitted to CPR and received rabies vaccine along with other immunizations during an eight-day hospital stay before discharge. Four days before his latest admission, he developed symptoms—reported hydrophobia-like signs when seeing water—and was readmitted on Thursday. He died on Saturday while still under treatment. The forest department was informed; officials said their six-month responsibility had ended. Dr. Sadanand Bhise of Rajarshi Shahu Chhatrapati Government Medical College, Kolhapur, said the exact cause cannot yet be determined pending a review of the patient file and treating doctors’ inputs. The article emphasizes administering rabies vaccine within 24 hours of a wolf bite.

article.articleHeadline: Centre steps up dengue surveillance as monsoon raises outbreak risk | Today News
article.articleSummary: Dengue surveillance in India is being intensified as the monsoon season creates favorable Aedes breeding conditions and potential El Niño-driven transmission risks. The health ministry has urged states to tighten dengue surveillance, expand laboratory testing with ELISA-based NS1 (first five days) and IgM kits, and boost larval source management with digital reporting via the IHIP-VBD portal. Hospitals should prepare contingency plans and rapid-response teams; ensure laboratories and insecticide stocks are functional. So far this year, 13,336 dengue cases and 12 deaths have been reported. Historically, India logged 121,824 cases and 131 deaths in 2025; 233,519/297 in 2024; and 289,235/485 in 2023. Tamil Nadu leads with 4,973 cases and 2 deaths; Maharashtra 1,525; Kerala 1,403 (10 deaths); Karnataka 978; Andhra Pradesh and West Bengal 770 each. Takeda’s dengue vaccine has been approved in India, expected next year, amid broader vector-borne disease mitigation including chikungunya and Zika.

article.articleHeadline: Travel and holidays: beware chikungunya and dengue — tips for those going to risk areas
article.articleSummary: Chikungunya and dengue are transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, with rising travel-related risk. Globally, chikungunya is reported in over 110 countries, with confirmed transmission in more than 50 in the last five years; dengue circulates across Africa, Southeast Asia, India, the Middle East, the Americas and Australia. Italy has seen local chikungunya foci in Veneto and Emilia-Romagna (last year) and autochthonous dengue in Lodi (2023) and Fano (2024). Chikungunya symptoms appear 3–7 days after a bite: fever, rash, fatigue and severe joint pain; chronic arthritis can follow; rare organ involvement. Dengue is often milder, but secondary infection with a different serotype can cause severe dengue; no specific cure exists for either. Prevention relies on repellents, long sleeves, light clothing, bed nets and daytime insecticides, since Aedes bites at dawn and dusk. Vaccines: chikungunya vaccine available in Italy since Oct 2025 for 12+, single dose 14 days before travel; dengue vaccine, for 4+, is two doses 3 months apart, no serology required, with strongest benefit for those previously infected. SIMVIM recommends vaccination for travelers to endemic areas, especially older adults, those with chronic disease, and pregnant women who cannot delay travel. Climate change and vector behavior may raise cases in Italy; inform travelers and maintain prevention.

article.articleHeadline: Mysterious bird deaths trigger bird flu fears in Karnataka's Koppal
article.articleSummary: Bird flu fears surge as mysterious deaths of birds in Karnataka's Koppal district prompt calls for investigation. Over the past three months thousands of egrets nested behind the Koppal City Municipal Council office, but in the past week dozens of birds die daily and many weakened birds are seen falling from trees. Residents fear a link to avian influenza amid drought-like conditions, though authorities have not confirmed any cause and no lab tests have been conducted (blood or tissue samples). Criticism mounts toward Municipal authorities and the Animal Husbandry Department for not inspecting the site. With Koppal hosting many poultry farms, locals urge urgent inspection by the Health Department, Animal Husbandry Department, and municipal authorities to rule out bird flu and protect public health and the poultry industry. No official confirmation yet of avian influenza.

article.articleHeadline: Jahanabad News: TB screening of 118,000 people conducted in Jahanabad.
article.articleSummary: As of August 2, 2026, Jehanabad district in Bihar, India completed TB screening of 118,804 residents under a TB elimination drive. High-risk groups underwent X-ray screening, with Jehanabad achieving the third-place ranking among Bihar districts for TB screening performance. The district administration notes the TB-free mission aims to identify and treat TB cases while ensuring patients receive proper nutrition and support to become fully healthy. In collaboration with Alkem Laboratories, all identified TB patients in the district will receive a TB Food and Nutrition Kit for six months to meet nutritional needs during treatment and bolster cure rates. The initiative underscores nutrition support as a critical component of TB care and aims to sustain treatment adherence and outcomes over the coming months.

article.articleHeadline: Chongqing Hot Pot Lovers, Beware Hepatitis E Knocking at Your Door! Chongqing Infectious Disease Expert Liu Min: Preventable and Curable.
article.articleSummary: Hepatitis E (HEV) outbreak in Chongqing, China. The Chongqing Health Commission reports rising HEV activity in 2026: 95 cases in February, and 99 cases in May–June. Pork-associated sources are key—undercooked pig liver and kidneys, pork products, shellfish, plus contaminated water and shared prep surfaces; hotpot dining heightens exposure. HEV incubation is 2–10 weeks. Early symptoms include fever, fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea; later dark urine and jaundice. Most adults recover with supportive care, but infection in late pregnancy carries 20–25% mortality, and elderly (over 45–60) and chronic liver disease increase risk (about 17.7% mortality with chronic liver disease). Immunocompromised individuals can become chronically infected. No specific antiviral exists; severe cases may require liver support. China-developed YikeNing (益可宁) vaccine—0,1,6 months—promises 100% efficacy during the full course and 86.6% after 10 years; recommended for pregnant women preconception, elderly, chronic liver disease patients, high‑risk workers, and travelers. Anti-HEV IgG testing guides immunity; vaccination status reviewed at Chongqing Public Health Center.

article.articleHeadline: Not only burns and fever: summer brings a hidden wave of infectious childhood diseases.
article.articleSummary: Summer conditions drive a hidden wave of infectious childhood diseases, notably hand, foot and mouth disease caused by Coxsackie viruses (enteroviruses), primarily affecting children under five. The infection is highly contagious and spreads through respiratory droplets and direct/contact with contaminated surfaces; the virus most often enters via the eyes, nose, or mouth. Incubation is 3–5 days. Early warning signs include dehydration (refusing fluids, reduced urination) and apathy, followed by fever, sore throat, painful oral ulcers, and a maculopapular rash on the palms and soles that can extend to knees, elbows, and buttocks. Summer activities—pools, camps, daycare—facilitate transmission, especially with hot temperatures that promote viral replication (China 2020 study cited). Management is supportive: antipyretics/analgesics and strict hydration; no specific antiviral treatment or vaccine. Most cases resolve in 7–10 days with good hygiene and rest.

article.articleHeadline: Man Swats Drain Fly Then Rubs Eye, Ends Up Losing An Eyeball To Severe Infection
article.articleSummary: In China, a man swatted a drain/moth fly that landed on his lower left eyelid and rubbed his eye, initially diagnosed as seasonal conjunctivitis. His condition rapidly worsened, with a Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection causing severe tissue damage around the eye and leading to enucleation of the left eyeball. Drain flies breed in damp, dirty areas and can carry bacteria such as E. coli, Salmonella, and P. aeruginosa. A separate report describes an eight-year-old girl with a digestive tract infection from moth fly larvae, likely after water splashing from a sink or toilet contaminated bathroom surfaces and exposure to her toothbrush/cup. Ophthalmologist Li of Peking University People’s Hospital notes two eye routes: the fly entering the eye and transferring bacteria/debris, or being crushed by hands. Management includes flushing the eye with artificial tears or saline, applying antibiotic drops if available, and seeking urgent care if pain, redness, or vision changes persist.

article.articleHeadline: Important! Henan Center for Disease Control and Prevention's Latest Advisory - NetEase Mobile
article.articleSummary: Henan Province’s Center for Disease Control and Prevention issued August risk guidance. With alternating high temperatures and heavy rains, humid conditions foster vectors and pathogens, while holiday travel raises exposure to vector-borne diseases and foodborne risks. Vector-borne diseases to watch include dengue fever, chikungunya fever, fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome, and malaria; prevention includes environmental management (eliminate standing water, seal containers, install screens) and personal protection (long sleeves, repellents, avoid peak mosquito times), and monitoring travel history to prevent imported cases. For food poisoning, the high-temperature, high-humidity season (May–October) increases microbial growth and toxins; ensure licensing checks, proper storage and hygiene, cook thoroughly, and seek care if symptoms occur. Extreme weather—heat waves, heavy rainfall, thunderstorms—requires heat prevention and flood safety with vigilance for warnings. Summer holidays demand reinforced supervision to prevent drowning, road, burn, and other injuries.

article.articleSummary: Cyclosporiasis outbreaks exceed 20,000 cases, with the total likely higher; CDC to update patient counts next week, and the source of the largest outbreak remains unidentified. Ineos Oxford Institute links the global spread of Campylobacter to industrial chicken farming, noting wild-bird–origin strains entering poultry flocks and rising antibiotic resistance. In South Korea, a study on raw fish consumption shows Kudoa septempunctata transmission from farmed olive flounder may be slowing after COVID-19-era dining restrictions. China reports mushroom poisonings reaching a six-year high in 2025, though fatalities were the lowest in that period. Zoonoses are diseases transmitted between animals and humans via direct/indirect contact or contaminated food and water.

article.articleHeadline: Yum! Brands stock rises despite Taco Bell outbreak
article.articleSummary: Cyclospora outbreak linked to shredded iceberg lettuce at Taco Bell across nine states caused 1,947 illnesses and 98 hospitalizations (no deaths) per CDC; FDA traced contamination to Taylor Farms de Mexico, with Taco Bell pulling the lettuce nationwide by July 17. Despite the scare, Yum! Brands stock rose 3% on July 30 after Q2 results that captured pre-outbreak strength. Q2 ended June 30: adjusted earnings $1.62 per share, vs $1.58 expected; revenue $2.17 billion, up 12% and near $2.2B. Management said the outbreak caused a meaningful but temporary sales decline; by July 27 Taco Bell location sales were down 2% in Q3-to-date, vs Q2 growth of 7%. Third-quarter margins expected 19–21% vs 26.2% in Q2. The industry framing as a farm-level problem limited fallout; Yum announced Pizza Hut sale for $2.7B, with LongRange Capital buying international units and Yum China acquiring the mainland piece, leaving KFC and Taco Bell core.

A Ming tale links hundreds of children in colored garments and banners reading 'The world is in chaos' to outbreaks. Daoist Zhang Daoling’s Celestial Masters lineage appears; envoy Xu Qi then averts Guangdong outbreak by letting people celebrate the New Year early and offering to gods. Lu Wan drives away demons; a virtuous widow is spared; a humane man buries the dead and saves a baby. Virtue governs fate; moral reflection can avert disaster.

article.articleHeadline: AFRICOM chief confirms US support for Laikipia Ebola quarantine facility
article.articleSummary: Ebola quarantine facility established at Laikipia Air Base in Kenya; AFRICOM confirms U.S. involvement in providing support while insisting the initiative was public health-led, not a military operation, with public health authorities and the Kenyan government in charge. Seven Americans, who worked in the Democratic Republic of Congo during the Ebola outbreak, are quarantining in Kenya after returning home; Samaritan’s Purse says they are under a 21‑day quarantine and have not developed symptoms. Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale had disputed reports that the seven were quarantined at the Laikipia site. The project previously faced a High Court halt and renewed protests in Nanyuki amid concerns about transparency, public participation, and Kenya’s role in the U.S. Ebola preparedness plan. The facility is described as part of Kenya’s public health preparedness and is not exclusive to U.S. citizens; questions remain about the agreement and agency responsibilities.

article.articleHeadline: Thermal cameras installed to strengthen Ebola surveillance at Bunia Airport - ACP.
article.articleSummary: Thermal cameras installed at Murongo Airport in Bunia, Ituri province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, aim to strengthen Ebola surveillance among travelers. The move, announced by Dr. Théophile Ponde, coordinator of the National Border Health Program (PNHF), adds to existing health measures including hand sanitizer dispensers and a digital traveler registration system using QR codes. The cameras screen for fever, one of the earliest Ebola symptoms, enabling rapid, non-contact detection and isolation of travelers with elevated temperatures. Data digitalization and QR-based recording are designed to improve entry-point surveillance and pre-empt local transmission. Travelers departing Bunia must pass through the registration system. The measures illustrate ongoing border health reinforcement against Ebola in an area already alert to potential outbreaks, with emphasis on early detection at air travel hubs.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in North Kivu: five ambulances out of thirty, no hearses out of twenty, two Ebola treatment centers meeting standards out of eleven.
article.articleSummary: North Kivu, Democratic Republic of Congo, reports degraded Ebola outbreak logistics as of July 30–31. Only 5 of 30 ambulances are functional; 0 of 20 hearses; 2 Ebola Treatment Centers (ETCs) meeting standards out of 11; no standard Transit Centers among 36. Isolation centers operate at 139% occupancy, with 27 confirmed and 169 suspected cases, plus 4 deaths and 2 recoveries. Cumulative confirmed admitted to treatment centers: 142 cases, 48 deaths (in-centre mortality 34%); 13 lost to follow-up. Provincial fatality is 66.4% (378 confirmed, 251 deaths), higher than Ituri’s 41.4%. On July 31, 12 new cases were reported in Beni, Katwa, Butembo, Kalunguta and Musienene; 9 deaths, including 5 in the community. Alerts total 1,033, with 852 investigated. Travelers screened: 59,834, 97.4% tested; 15 of 16 border posts transmitted data. Contact tracing at 74.7% (below 95%). Actions include supplies to Musienene, medicines from health program, UNFPA dignity kits; urgent ETC expansion; two health facilities burned in Butembo.

article.articleSummary: On 2 August 2026, in Beni, North Kivu, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, a woman ill with Ebola who sparked Saturday clashes at the La Joie medical center was referred to an Ebola treatment center. The patient was described as agonizing, and a center official termed the scene war-like, with projectiles and police warnings; protesters damaged an ambulance. The disturbances led to the suspension of Ebola response activities at the health center and at a new treatment center under construction, forcing workers to return home. The Ebola response coordination deployed teams to sensitize the population about the dangers of the virus and to counter pressure groups opposing the outbreak. This incident underscores ongoing security challenges amid Ebola response efforts in Beni.

article.articleHeadline: Zoonosis: From Animals to Humans
article.articleSummary: Thirteen hantavirus cases and three deaths occurred on the cruise MV Hondius; the World Health Organization declared the outbreak finished after the last exposed person completed quarantine and tested negative. Ebola remains a major concern: a Bundibugyo outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, declared May 15, has caused 399 deaths and 1,333 confirmed cases, with spread to Uganda (20 cases, 2 deaths). MSF notes overwhelmed treatment centers in Ituri and late patient presentation. Six Ebola strains are identified (Zaire, Sudan, Bundibugyo, Taï Forest, Reston, Bombali). Hantavirus Andes is the outbreak-linked strain; European/Asian hantaviruses can cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, while American hantaviruses cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome with 20–40% fatality. Rabies causes about 59,000 deaths annually, mainly via dog bites; incubation typically 3–8 weeks, and post-exposure prophylaxis remains critical.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue cases rise in Cebu City
article.articleSummary: Dengue in Cebu City, Philippines, recorded 1,228 cases and 10 deaths from Jan 1 to July 18, 2026, a 12.35% rise from 1,093 cases. The case fatality rate is 0.81% as Cebu City remains under DOH endemic classification, not at alert or epidemic thresholds. Officials attribute the increase to persistent rains that clog drainage and create stagnant water, with garbage hindering water flow and boosting Aedes breeding. Ages range from 2 months to 96 years, median 12; children 1–10 years account for about 498 cases (40.55%), while males total 661 (53.83%). From July 12–18, 17 new cases followed a Morbidity Week 26 peak of 78. Highest barangays by cases include Guadalupe and Basak San Nicolas. Mortality spread across districts; hospitals include Cebu City Medical Center (5) and Vicente Sotto Memorial Medical Center (1) among others. City promotes the DOH 5S dengue prevention strategy and school-based 'Search and Destroy' measures.

article.articleHeadline: Rising Tides, Surge In Cases: Fiji, Philippines Face Unprecedented HIV Epidemics Amid Global Funding Cuts | OneNews.PH
article.articleSummary: Fiji is experiencing the world's fastest-growing HIV epidemic, with about 12,000 people living with HIV in a population under 1 million. In Fiji, one in 60 adults is HIV-positive; infections among women are rising, and roughly one child is born with HIV each week and one dies from HIV-related complications each month. In the Philippines, 4,633 new diagnoses and an estimated 288,000 living with HIV; daily cases average 51–57, with 15–34-year-olds about 80% of new infections. Both miss the 95-95-95 targets; global funding cuts threaten responses. Fiji receives support from Australia and New Zealand; the Philippines from the United States and local groups. Community-led approaches and regional lessons from Africa are urged to sustain momentum as of 3 August 2026.

article.articleHeadline: Kendari Regional Secretary Opens HIV/AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria Control Partnership Forum.
article.articleSummary: On August 2, 2026, Kendari City Secretary opened a Partnership Forum to accelerate control of HIV/AIDS, Tuberculosis (TB), and Malaria in Kendari, Southeast Sulawesi, Indonesia. The event emphasizes cross-sector collaboration beyond the health sector, with participation from government agencies, private sector, civil society organizations, and communities to strengthen prevention and care systems. The forum aims to harmonize work programs, improve early detection, and provide patient support to ensure complete treatment, while addressing social stigma that hinders access to services. Officials highlighted commitment to national elimination targets for HIV/AIDS, TB, and malaria, and discussed more effective use of resources and budgeting, including data validation for policy decisions and efficient distribution of medicines. Attendees included the Health Department, other regional government agencies, and health development partners, with expectations that outcomes translate into concrete actions to improve public health in Kendari.

article.articleHeadline: Expert Column: Lung Virus at PIR PDPI.
article.articleSummary: At the Pertemuan Ilmiah Respirasi (PIR) of the Indonesian Pulmonology Association (PDPI) in Cirebon, on August 1, 2026, Prof. Tjandra delivered a plenary lecture to about 300 attendees from West Java and neighboring regions. He outlined eight globally relevant respiratory viruses that could already be present in Indonesia: avian influenza, seasonal influenza, Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus (MERS-CoV), Nipah virus disease, hantavirus infection, COVID-19, Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), and Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV). The talk underscores the rising burden of pulmonary diseases in West Java and stresses that future pandemics are possible, though the timing and causative agents are unknown. The article does not report laboratory-confirmed outbreaks, infection sources, or specifics on imported/exported cases. The emphasis remains on preparedness for viral respiratory diseases as a looming pandemic risk rather than on a particular outbreak.

article.articleHeadline: Deli Serdang Regency Government Accelerates TB Elimination, Targets 100,000 Detected Cases
article.articleSummary: Deli Serdang Regency, North Sumatra, Indonesia, launches an accelerated TB elimination campaign from August 1 to October 31, 2026, targeting the detection of at least 100,000 TB cases through integrated Free Health Check (Cek Kesehatan Gratis, CKG). The plan uses 480 loci, each screening about 100 people (initial ~48,000 screened) with a goal of 100,000 detections to hasten elimination by 2030 as part of the Generasi Emas 2045 initiative. Collaboration includes private hospitals/clinics and village heads under district authorities; focus areas include Percut Sei Tuan, notably Sei Rotan village, due to higher TB incidence. Mobile X-ray-equipped service cars will conduct door-to-door screening, emphasizing contacts and household contacts. The program integrates CKG, TB elimination, and the Three Million Homes (Tiga Juta Rumah) initiative, and provides comprehensive support: nutrition, housing improvements (bedah rumah), and patient accompaniment to ensure treatment completion while reducing stigma.

article.articleHeadline: South Africa hopeful of possible TB vaccine breakthrough
article.articleSummary: South Africa is preparing for potential rollout of the M27 tuberculosis vaccine, aiming to align registration and introduction promptly if ongoing trials demonstrate safety and efficacy. The department targets TB elimination as a public health threat by 2030, with M27 already showing promise in Phase I/II and currently in Phase III trials in South Africa, Kenya, Zambia, Malawi, and Indonesia. If SAHPRA approves the vaccine, it would mark the first new TB vaccine in more than a century, offering protection for adolescents and adults. Early preparations seek to prevent delays in vaccine access for communities. Global partners, including the Gates Medical Research Institute and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, have an agreement with the Serum Institute of India to manufacture and supply doses worldwide, potentially enabling local manufacturing partnerships in South Africa and Indonesia.

article.articleHeadline: Rise in HIV Infections in Brazil Demands More from the Authorities.
article.articleSummary: HIV infections in Brazil rose 21.9% from 2010 to 2024, against a global 43% drop in new infections and a worldwide HIV population of about 41 million, including 1.7 million in Brazil. UNAIDS cautions the world will miss the 2030 target to reduce new infections and AIDS deaths by 90%; annual deaths declined 57% to roughly 570,000, still 400,000 above the target. Scientific tools—safe-sex campaigns, antiretroviral therapy (ART), and pre/post-exposure prophylaxis—exist, but sustained public policies are essential. Brazil, once a regional exemplar for HIV response, now ranks among countries with rising infections. Globally, mother-to-child transmission prevention reached 87% in 2025 (vs. 24% a decade-and-a-half earlier), ART coverage reached 78% (vs. 24% then). Brazil’s 95-95-95 indicators are 96-82-95. Gaps in treatment initiation, monitoring, and continuity demand active case finding and uninterrupted drug supply within the SUS framework.

article.articleHeadline: An International Organization: Al-Ubayyid on the Brink of a Humanitarian Catastrophe Amid Water Shortages and a Cholera Outbreak - Sudan News
article.articleSummary: Al-Ubayyid, in North Kordofan, Sudan, is on the brink of a humanitarian catastrophe due to a cholera outbreak, severe water shortages, and food insecurity. Plan International reports a 70% water-supply gap as main sources are out of service amid siege and Rapid Support Forces attacks, with displacement swelling the population. The city hosts about 105,000 internally displaced people in camps and shelters; health centers and sanitation infrastructure are heavily damaged, compounded by rainfall and poor hygiene in camps. Recently, the army recaptured Barra and Jabra al-Sheikh and other sites along the export road to deter a RSF ground assault, but the area remains under drone strikes. Plan International calls for urgent international action to protect children, warning of malnutrition, gender-based violence at water points, and risk of child recruitment. The NGO continues life-saving aid despite power, water, and food disruptions and restricted access.

article.articleHeadline: Cuiabá Intensifies Monitoring of Zoonotic Diseases and Maintains Active Surveillance to Protect the Population
article.articleSummary: Cuiabá's Municipal Health Secretariat (SMS) maintains environmental and epidemiological surveillance to monitor zoonoses. In the first half of 2026, 88 epizootic notifications were recorded, focused on primates and wild birds as sentinels for yellow fever and avian influenza. Visceral leishmaniasis was the most frequent canine disease, with 782 inspections and 249 confirmed canine cases; one human case was confirmed. Sporotrichosis appeared in cats (21 notifications, 17 lab-confirmed); 13 human suspects with 6 confirmations. Rabies surveillance remained intense: 62 notifications of dead or neurologically affected animals, 6 veterinary visits for suspicious behavior, and 52 companion animals with bat contact. The human side recorded 753 anti-rabies consultations, 125 severe cases. Yellow fever epizootics in 14 monkeys were suspected but none confirmed. Avian influenza IAAP investigations in two areas yielded five wild-bird notifications; all negative, no human cases. Authorities urge reporting abnormal animal behavior and vaccination of pets; seek post-exposure care after bites.

article.articleHeadline: Parasite that feeds on living animals drives the U.S. to invest millions.
article.articleSummary: New World screwworm fly infestation prompts a US$25 million USDA investment to curb the parasite that feeds on living tissue. A sterile-insect technique will release millions of sterile males to mate with wild females, reducing reproduction. A new distribution unit will operate in Douglas, Arizona, near the US–Mexico border, to accelerate responses, alongside a large-scale production facility in Texas. The larvae infest wounds in cattle, sheep, goats, horses, and other warm-blooded animals, causing tissue destruction, secondary infections, weight loss, stress, and potentially death; wildlife and domestic pets can also be affected, with human cases rare. The strategy aims to bolster border defenses as new foci arise in Central America and Mexico, and to ease import restrictions on Mexican cattle gradually, with Douglas first to reopen. Brazil monitors closely, advising vigilant inspections and early diagnoses.

article.articleHeadline: Leukemia, AIDS, Canine Distemper, and Mange: Diseases Transmitted by Domestic Dogs and Cats Threaten Wild Felines | Environmental Readings
article.articleSummary: Domestic dogs and cats in Latin America are transmitting viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites to wild felids, threatening jaguars, pumas, ocelots, margays, oncillas, jaguarundis. Diseases include feline leukemia virus (FeLV), feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV, 'feline AIDS'), feline panleukopenia (FPV), canine distemper virus (CDV), rabies, and mange. In Mexico's Chamela-Cuixmala reserve, a jaguar death could mean a 20% local population loss. In Ecuador, 87.5% of ocelots tested FeLV positive and 23.5% CDV positive. In Bolivia, a wild cat raised in captivity contracted panleucopenia and died. In Chile, colocolo cats face FeLV and antibiotic-resistant bacteria. In Brazil, jaguar, puma, ocelot, and pampas cat populations face FeLV, FIV, FPV, rabies, CDV, and other infections due to habitat loss increasing contact with domestic animals. In Costa Rica, the La Amenaza Invisible project detected FeLV and FIV in pets near wild felids, prompting calls for vaccination and surveillance.

article.articleHeadline: The storm passes through MS, but contaminated water continues to pose a risk of disease.
article.articleSummary: Following heavy rains in Campo Grande, Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil, flooding raised water- and waste-related disease risks. The city recorded 102.4 mm of rain in 24 hours—the nation's highest—before waters receded. Health experts warn that floodwater, mud and debris can transmit leptospirosis, cholera, hepatitis and typhoid fever, and that post- flood conditions favor Aedes aegypti breeding, with Campo Grande reporting 1,354 dengue and 36 chikungunya cases so far this year. Protective guidance includes wearing boots, gloves and long clothing during cleanup, inspecting footwear and clothing, removing debris, eliminating standing water, and storing potable water in closed containers; any foods touched by floodwater should be discarded. Do not attempt to capture venomous wildlife; seek medical care for bites or stings. Prompt medical evaluation is advised for anyone with fever, body pains, diarrhea or vomiting after floodwater exposure, or for wounds.

article.articleHeadline: Leprosy, cases are rising in Florida: what this means for Italy and why experts are urging not to lower your guard.
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-08-02, Florida reports 36 leprosy cases, renewing attention to a disease that remains global, curable. Leprosy (Hansen’s disease) in Florida highlights a suspected reservoir in the nine-banded armadillo, with soil exposure and occupations like gardening as possible routes; casual contact with armadillos or soil does not automatically transmit the disease. The WHO notes leprosy was never eradicated; in 2000 it was declared eliminated as a public health problem (less than 1 per 10,000). Roughly 170,000 cases occur worldwide, led by India, with Brazil and Indonesia as major hotspots; other high-burden countries include Bangladesh, Madagascar, Nepal, Nigeria, and South Sudan. Europe sees mostly imported cases. OMS strategies include contact tracing with rifampicin preventive therapy, Leprosy Elimination Framework for mapping, and free multidrug therapy for 6–12 months, with contagiousness reduced after initial doses. Incubation can reach 3–5 years; early signs are hypopigmented patches with sensory loss. Italy’s risk remains extremely low.

article.articleHeadline: Paying a heavy price for 20 years of untreated hepatitis B infection, and spreading it to the entire family.
article.articleSummary: Hepatitis B virus infection can silently persist in the liver for decades, eventually causing cirrhosis, liver failure, and cancer if untreated. At Bach Mai Hospital in Hanoi, a 53-year-old man diagnosed 20 years ago stopped antiviral therapy after feeling better; two decades later he has cirrhosis, ascites, esophageal varices, peritoneal infection, and requires dialysis. His wife and children were later found infected, underscoring family transmission. In Nam Dinh Province, two brothers infected by their mother illustrate divergent outcomes: the elder adheres to treatment and vaccination, staying well and preventing spread; the younger, diagnosed at 45, has transmitted to his wife and son. Experts urge regular HBV DNA testing, liver fibrosis assessment, and continued antiviral therapy; vaccinating and screening household contacts, and preventing mother-to-child transmission via prenatal management and timely neonatal vaccination.

article.articleHeadline: Strict control, no room for complacency with avian influenza
article.articleSummary: Avian influenza A(H5N1) outbreaks persist in Vietnam, with Hà Tĩnh province reporting a local cluster in Cam Duệ commune. Since July 13, 2026, 228 poultry across five households were infected; 120 chickens from one family were culled, and barns disinfected. Authorities vaccinated more than 15,600 birds across three hamlets (Quốc Tiến, Na Trung, Trần Phú), posted warning signs, and applied lime powder and disinfectants in containment zones. Nationwide, Vietnam has recorded 80 outbreaks in 73 communes across 17 provinces, with more than 349,400 poultry dying or being culled. Nghệ An, a neighboring province, shows rising outbreak activity. Hà Tĩnh reports a large total poultry stock (~10 million) and challenges including low first-round vaccination coverage and incomplete disease reporting on some farms. Officials urge intensified surveillance, supplementary H5N1 vaccination, biosafety, reporting, and strict monitoring of live poultry markets to prevent year-end spread.

article.articleHeadline: 🐚 Laos pushes back parasitic disease to below one percent
article.articleSummary: Schistosomiasis in Laos has fallen to under 1% prevalence in the worst-affected areas, down from over 40% in 2003, with Champasack Province remaining the last transmission focus and about 120,000 people in 202 villages at risk. In 2024, over 95,000 individuals received a yearly single-dose treatment that clears the parasite and halts transmission. The snail-borne disease, spread by freshwater snails in water used for washing, fishing, and transport along the Mekong River, can cause enlarged liver and bleeding during toileting, with severe cases leading to fatal liver damage. The program combines mass treatment, water/sanitation improvements, and health education, with strengthened surveillance by China’s NIPD and the Swiss Tropical/Public Health Institute. Cross-border collaboration with Cambodia and support from WHO, China, and Switzerland totaling about $1.18 million underpins progress. Malaria fell to 272 cases in 2025.

article.articleHeadline: Ear swelling, a 60-year-old man in critical condition due to necrotizing fasciitis
article.articleSummary: A 60-year-old man admitted to Phu Tho General Hospital in Vietnam with progressive swelling around the right ear due to a salivary-gland abscess and fever. About a week earlier a small lump appeared; self-medication failed to help, and swelling increased. Clinicians diagnosed spreading cellulitis with an abscess; surgical drainage was performed and pus cultured. Culture identified Burkholderia pseudomallei, the agent of Whitmore disease (melioidosis). He was transferred to the Tropical Diseases Ward and started on antibiotics per susceptibility testing, with supportive care. Fever resolved and the abscess reduced markedly, with good response to therapy. Melioidosis is a dangerous infection that can cause bacteremia and multi‑organ damage, with high mortality if not diagnosed and treated. The bacterium is endemic in tropical regions, especially Southeast Asia and northern Australia, acquired via skin breaks or inhalation. Early lab confirmation and targeted antibiotics improve outcomes.

article.articleHeadline: Center for Medical Science conducts random screening of Nile tilapia and giant river prawn; finds antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
article.articleSummary: Thailand’s Center for Medical Science conducted random screening of Nile tilapia and giant river prawn, finding antibiotic‑resistant bacteria linked to environmental contamination and improper antimicrobial use in aquaculture. Consumers are advised to cook fish and shellfish thoroughly to reduce risk, with findings supporting integrated water monitoring and environmental management across supply chains. Environmental and economically important species—Nile tilapia, sea bass, giant river prawn, white shrimp, and black tiger shrimp—were tested for food-safety pathogens including E. coli and Salmonella, and other bacteria. Salmonella prevalence in aquaculture is <5%; no carbapenem resistance detected. Antimicrobial use in aquaculture has fallen >60% from 2017 to 2023; about 68.69% of farmers and staff practice rational antimicrobial use. Thailand’s AMR mortality is ~38,000/year (global ~1.27 million), with >40 billion THB annual economic loss. ONE HEALTH-based targets aim for a 10% reduction in AMR deaths by 2030.

article.articleHeadline: Watch out for ticks - they carry viruses such as the Bourbon virus.
article.articleSummary: Bourbon virus, a rare RNA virus in the Orthomyxoviridae family (thogotovirus), was first identified in Kansas in 2014. Transmission to humans occurs solely via tick bites, with no evidence of human-to-human spread. The primary vector is the lone star tick, Amblyomma americanum, which has no stable populations in Europe or Russia and is not endemic there. A rare New York case revived concern, but there is no confirmed Bourbon virus circulation on European or Russian soil. Infected individuals typically develop high fever, severe weakness, headache, myalgia, nausea/vomiting, and rash, with leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. There is no vaccine or specific antiviral therapy; care is supportive. Other tick-borne diseases are present in Europe and Eurasia: Greece reports Lyme disease and tick-borne encephalitis from local ticks, not Bourbon virus; Russia has Ixodes persulcatus and I. ricinus spreading tick-borne encephalitis and borreliosis, while Hyalomma in southern areas can transmit Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever.

article.articleHeadline: Climate change shifts malaria risk to southern, East Africa: Study
article.articleSummary: Malaria risk in Africa is shifting with climate change. The Nature study on childhood malaria in sub-Saharan Africa finds a slight overall increase but a reallocation of risk by region. In current hotspots—West Africa (Nigeria, Burkina Faso, Mali)—malaria cases may drop about 5% as temperatures rise, with Niger, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, and Somalia potentially approaching elimination. Conversely, cooler regions such as southern Africa and high-elevation East Africa are becoming more suitable for mosquitoes, with about a 5% rise in the Ethiopian highlands (Kenya, Burundi) and similar increases in Angola, Zambia, and northeast South Africa; by 2100, Rift Valley and coastal southern Africa could see roughly a 20% rise. Limiting warming to 2°C could avert ~5 excess cases per 1,000 children in southern Africa and more in east African highlands. Adaptation and elimination efforts are emphasized as essential.
